title: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
description: Grade 6 Science: separating mixtures by hand-picking, winnowing, sedimentation, decantation, filtration and evaporation. Notes, solved examples and a test.

topics.title: Why and How We Separate Mixtures; Hand-picking and Winnowing
topics.concept:
When two or more substances are mixed together without forming a new substance, we get a mixture — for example, rice with small stones, or tea leaves in tea. In daily life we often need to separate the things in a mixture. We do this to remove harmful or useless parts (stones from rice), to get a useful part (cream from milk), or to remove impurities (mud from water).

The method we choose depends on the properties of the things being separated — their size, weight, whether they dissolve, and so on. Two simple hand methods are:

  • Hand-picking — simply picking out the unwanted bits by hand. It works when the pieces are large enough to see and few enough to remove, and look different — like taking stones, husk or insects out of rice, wheat or pulses.
  • Winnowing — separating heavier grains from lighter husk using wind or by blowing air. The mixture is allowed to fall from a height; the wind carries the light husk away to one side, while the heavier grain falls straight down into a heap. Farmers use winnowing to separate grain from chaff after harvesting.

examples.problem: Example 1: Which method would you use to remove a few small stones from a bowl of rice, and why?
examples.solution:
Choose the method that suits large, visible, few pieces.

  • The stones are big enough to see and few in number.
  • So they can simply be picked out by hand — hand-picking.
examples.answer: Hand-picking, because the stones are large and few enough to see and remove by hand.

examples.problem: Example 2: How does winnowing separate grain from husk?
examples.solution:
Winnowing uses the difference in weight and wind.

  • The mixture is dropped from a height in the wind.
  • The light husk is blown away to one side; the heavy grain falls straight down.
examples.answer: The wind blows the lighter husk away while the heavier grain falls straight down, separating the two.

examples.problem: Example 3: On what does the choice of a separation method mainly depend?
examples.solution:
We pick a method to match the substances.

  • It depends on the properties of the things to be separated, such as size and weight.
examples.answer: It depends on the properties (such as size and weight) of the substances being separated.

recap:
• A mixture is two or more substances mixed without forming a new substance.
  • We separate mixtures to remove harmful/useless parts or to obtain a useful part.
  • Hand-picking removes large, few, visible pieces by hand.
  • Winnowing uses wind to separate lighter husk from heavier grain.

quiz.q: Separating heavier grain from lighter husk using wind is called:
quiz.explanation: Winnowing uses wind to blow away the lighter husk.

quiz.q: Hand-picking is suitable when the pieces to be removed are:
quiz.explanation: Hand-picking works for large, few, visible pieces.

topics.title: Sedimentation, Decantation and Filtration
topics.concept:
Some mixtures are of a solid with a liquid, where the solid does not dissolve — like muddy water. To separate these we use settling and straining methods.

  • Sedimentation — when a mixture of an insoluble solid and a liquid is left undisturbed, the heavier solid particles slowly settle to the bottom. The settled solid is called sediment. For example, mud settles at the bottom of a glass of muddy water.
  • Decantation — after the solid has settled, the clear liquid on top is gently poured off into another container without disturbing the sediment. Sedimentation is almost always followed by decantation.
  • Filtration — passing a mixture through a filter (such as filter paper, a cloth or a sieve) that has tiny holes. The liquid and very fine particles pass through, while the larger insoluble solid is trapped on the filter. The clear liquid that passes through is called the filtrate, and the solid left behind is the residue.

We use these methods every day: tea is poured through a strainer to hold back the leaves (filtration); and at home, muddy water can be cleaned by letting the mud settle (sedimentation), pouring off the clear water (decantation) and then filtering it.

examples.problem: Example 1: Muddy water is left still for some time and the mud collects at the bottom. Name this process and the settled solid.
examples.solution:
Heavier insoluble particles settle when left undisturbed.

  • The process is sedimentation.
  • The settled solid is called sediment.
examples.answer: The process is sedimentation; the settled solid is called sediment.

examples.problem: Example 2: When tea is poured through a strainer, what passes through and what is left behind? Name the method.
examples.solution:
A strainer is a filter with tiny holes.

  • The liquid tea (filtrate) passes through; the tea leaves (residue) are held back.
  • This is filtration.
examples.answer: The liquid tea passes through (filtrate) and the tea leaves are held back (residue); the method is filtration.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is decantation, and which process usually comes just before it?
examples.solution:
Decantation pours off the clear liquid after settling.

  • It is gently pouring off the clear liquid without disturbing the sediment.
  • It usually follows sedimentation.
examples.answer: Decantation is gently pouring off the clear upper liquid; it usually follows sedimentation.

recap:
• Sedimentation: heavier insoluble solids settle to the bottom as sediment when left undisturbed.
  • Decantation: gently pouring off the clear liquid above the sediment.
  • Filtration: passing a mixture through a filter; liquid (filtrate) passes, solid (residue) is trapped.
  • These methods clean muddy water and separate tea leaves, etc.

quiz.q: The settling of heavier insoluble particles to the bottom is called:
quiz.explanation: Sedimentation is the settling of insoluble solids to the bottom.

quiz.q: In filtration, the clear liquid that passes through the filter is called the:
quiz.explanation: The liquid that passes through the filter is the filtrate.

topics.title: Evaporation as a Method of Separation
topics.concept:
The methods so far separate insoluble solids from liquids. But what if a solid is dissolved in a liquid, like salt in water? You cannot filter it out, because the dissolved salt passes straight through the filter with the water. For this we use evaporation.

In evaporation, the solution (for example salt water) is heated gently or left in the Sun. The water turns into vapour and escapes into the air, leaving the solid behind. This is exactly how common salt is obtained from sea water: sea water is collected in shallow pans, the Sun evaporates the water, and the salt is left behind to be collected. This is called solar evaporation.

Often we use more than one method together to fully separate a mixture. For example, to get clean salt and clean water from a mixture of sand, salt and water: first filter to remove the insoluble sand (the residue), then evaporate the salt water to obtain the salt. Choosing the right method — or combination of methods — for each property of a mixture is the key skill of this chapter.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why can salt dissolved in water NOT be separated by filtration?
examples.solution:
Filtration only traps solids that do not dissolve.

  • Dissolved salt breaks into tiny particles that pass through the filter with the water.
  • So filtration cannot remove it.
examples.answer: Because the dissolved salt passes through the filter along with the water; we must use evaporation instead.

examples.problem: Example 2: Describe how common salt is obtained from sea water.
examples.solution:
Salt is left behind when water evaporates.

  • Sea water is collected in shallow pans.
  • The Sun evaporates the water, leaving the salt behind to be collected.
examples.answer: Sea water is left in shallow pans where the Sun evaporates the water, leaving the salt behind to collect.

examples.problem: Example 3: Which two methods, and in what order, would you use to separate sand and salt from a mixture of sand, salt and water?
examples.solution:
Sand is insoluble; salt is dissolved.

  • First filter to remove the insoluble sand (residue).
  • Then evaporate the salt water to get the salt.
examples.answer: First filtration (to remove the sand), then evaporation (to get the salt) — in that order.

recap:
• Evaporation separates a dissolved solid from a liquid: the liquid escapes as vapour, the solid stays behind.
  • It cannot be done by filtration because dissolved solids pass through the filter.
  • Common salt is obtained from sea water by solar evaporation.
  • Often several methods are combined (e.g. filtration then evaporation) to fully separate a mixture.

quiz.q: To separate salt that is dissolved in water, we use:
quiz.explanation: Evaporation removes the water and leaves the dissolved salt behind.

quiz.q: Common salt is obtained from sea water mainly by:
quiz.explanation: Sun evaporates the sea water, leaving the salt behind.

questions.q: Two or more substances mixed without forming a new substance make a:
questions.explanation: Substances simply mixed together form a mixture.

questions.q: The method of separation we use mainly depends on the ___ of the substances.
questions.explanation: We choose a method based on properties like size, weight and solubility.

questions.q: Removing a few visible stones from rice by hand is called:
questions.explanation: Picking out large, few, visible bits by hand is hand-picking.

questions.q: Separating lighter husk from heavier grain using wind is:
questions.explanation: Winnowing uses wind to carry away the lighter husk.

questions.q: When muddy water is left still, the mud settles to the bottom. This is:
questions.explanation: Insoluble solids settling to the bottom is sedimentation.

questions.q: The solid that settles at the bottom during sedimentation is called the:
questions.explanation: The settled solid is the sediment.

questions.q: Gently pouring off the clear liquid above the settled solid is:
questions.explanation: Pouring off the clear upper liquid is decantation.

questions.q: Passing a mixture through filter paper or a sieve is called:
questions.explanation: Filtration passes liquid through a filter and traps the solid.

questions.q: In filtration, the clear liquid that passes through is the:
questions.explanation: The liquid passing through the filter is the filtrate.

questions.q: In filtration, the solid trapped on the filter is the:
questions.explanation: The solid held back on the filter is the residue.

questions.q: When tea is poured through a strainer, the strainer acts as a:
questions.explanation: A strainer with tiny holes is a filter; this is filtration.

questions.q: Salt dissolved in water cannot be separated by filtration because the salt:
options: Passes through the filter with the water
questions.explanation: Dissolved salt passes through the filter, so filtration cannot remove it.

questions.q: To separate dissolved salt from water we use:
questions.explanation: Evaporation removes the water and leaves the salt behind.

questions.q: Common salt is obtained from sea water using the Sun's heat by:
questions.explanation: Solar evaporation leaves the salt behind as the sea water evaporates.

questions.q: To separate sand, salt and water, you should first ___ and then ___.
options: filter to remove sand, then evaporate to get salt
questions.explanation: Filter out the insoluble sand first, then evaporate the salt water to obtain the salt.

questions.q: A mixture of iron filings, sand and salt is to be fully separated. The BEST first step is to:
options: Use a magnet to remove the iron filings
questions.explanation: A magnet quickly removes the magnetic iron filings first, using a property of the material.

questions.q: After the iron is removed, water is added to the sand-and-salt mixture. Filtering it gives:
options: Sand as residue and salt water as filtrate
Salt as residue and sand as filtrate
questions.explanation: Insoluble sand is trapped as residue; the dissolved salt passes through in the filtrate.

questions.q: Winnowing works because grain and husk differ mainly in their:
questions.explanation: The light husk is blown further than the heavy grain, so the difference in weight separates them.

questions.q: Sedimentation followed by decantation is used to begin cleaning:
questions.explanation: The mud settles (sedimentation) and the clear water is poured off (decantation).

questions.q: Why is filtration alone NOT enough to make muddy river water safe to drink?
options: It removes only larger dirt, not dissolved impurities or germs
questions.explanation: Filtration removes visible dirt but not dissolved impurities or tiny germs, so further treatment (like boiling) is needed.

questions.q: A salt solution is evaporated to dryness. What is left in the dish?
questions.explanation: The water escapes as vapour, leaving the salt behind in the dish.
